headline: Your US tech holdings took a hit last night — MSFT and GOOG both down 4%+ — while the ASX closed green and oil surged on Middle East tensions, lifting FUEL.

portfolio.summary: Your portfolio sits at $1,909 AUD, essentially flat against your $1,912 invested — you're only $2.62 in the red overall, which is remarkably steady. The real story is the tug-of-war: your US holdings (TTWO, MSFT) are dragging while your ASX ETFs are holding firm. TTWO is your biggest dollar loser at -$19.91 AUD below your buy-in, and MSFT has slipped just -$1.59 AUD underwater. On the bright side, GOOG is still up $16.76 AUD (+24%) since you bought in — the best performer in the portfolio by percentage despite last night's dip. FUEL is your ASX standout today, up $5.73 AUD on the back of surging oil prices.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Dropped $19.21 USD last night — that's your biggest single-session dollar move. You're now just $1.59 AUD underwater on your MSFT position overall. Microsoft unveiled new in-house AI models to reduce its reliance on OpenAI, which may have spooked investors worried about partnership dynamics.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Fell $14.19 USD last night. Despite the drop, you're still up $16.76 AUD (+24%) on your GOOG position from your buy-in — one of the portfolio's brightest spots. Commentary is circling about Google lagging OpenAI and Anthropic in the AI race, which is weighing on the stock.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Down $4.60 USD last night, and sitting $19.91 AUD below what you paid — the portfolio's biggest dollar loss. GTA 6 hype continues but hasn't translated into a share price catalyst yet.

movers.name: BetaShares Global Energy ETF
movers.note: Closed up $0.15 AUD today to $8.70, putting you $5.73 AUD ahead of your buy-in. Oil jumped over 2.6% last night on Iran-US tensions and the IEA warning about critically low stockpiles heading into peak summer demand — great news for this holding.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: Ticked up 50 cents today to $76.65 — you're $2.53 AUD ahead of what you invested. Steady as she goes with the ASX broadly green today.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: Up $2.38 AUD today to $522.55, putting you $2.99 AUD in the green. The ASX-listed version tracked well despite the US tech weakness from last night.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 had a solid session today, closing up 0.7% at 8,785 — a gain of about 61 points. Last night's US session was basically flat: the S&P 500 edged up just 0.13% and the NASDAQ barely moved (+0.03%), so the broader index calm masks some nasty individual stock moves in tech. The big story is oil — WTI crude jumped 2.6% to $96.22 USD a barrel, driven by Iran-US military strikes and Middle East conflict. Gold is steady at $4,486 USD. The Aussie dollar is sitting at 71.59 US cents, barely changed.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session — barely moved overall.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Last night — flat index masks big drops in GOOG and MSFT individually.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Surged on Iran-US strikes and IEA supply warnings.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Essentially unchanged — holding near record highs.

politics.summary: The Australian economy is front and centre today, with fresh GDP data showing 2.5% annual growth but a slowdown clearly beginning. The RBA and Treasurer Chalmers are both pointing fingers at interest rates and tax as culprits for falling house prices, and there's growing debate about whether the rate-hiking cycle is finally over.

stories.title: Australia's economy growing at 2.5% annually — but the slowdown is starting
stories.why_it_matters: The latest national accounts show the Aussie economy is growing at 2.5% annually, but momentum is fading. The combination of higher interest rates and cost-of-living pressure is starting to bite households and businesses alike. For investors, a slowing economy typically means the RBA has less reason to keep hiking rates — which would be good news for shares and property. Watch for the RBA's next move carefully.

stories.title: Stalling economy could stop further interest rate hikes
stories.why_it_matters: Analysts are now arguing the slowing economy gives the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA — the body that sets our interest rates) a clear reason to pause or stop raising rates. If the RBA stops hiking, that's a relief for mortgage holders and generally supportive for growth stocks and property values. The 'war bite' referenced is the ongoing Middle East conflict weighing on global trade and confidence.

stories.title: RBA and Chalmers blame interest rates and tax for house price falls
stories.why_it_matters: Both the RBA and Treasurer Jim Chalmers are now openly acknowledging that higher interest rates and the tax system are contributing to falling house prices. This is a notable admission — it signals both sides of the political/economic divide accept the rate cycle is doing real damage to the property market. For property-owning Aussies, this is validation that the pain is real. For investors, it reinforces the case for rates to peak soon.

stories.title: Labor MPs asked to fund campaign to salvage budget
stories.why_it_matters: Labor MPs are reportedly being asked to personally contribute to a political advertising campaign to help the government defend its budget position. This is unusual — it suggests internal concern about public perception of the budget and the government's economic management. It's a sign of political pressure building heading into the next phase of the parliamentary term.

ai.summary: The dominant AI story today is Trump's executive order (a presidential directive) that introduces a pre-approval process for AI models from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic before they can launch. Meanwhile, Microsoft made a notable move to build its own AI models so it's less dependent on OpenAI, and commentary is getting louder that Google is falling behind its rivals.

stories.title: Trump's new AI executive order: pre-checks for OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic before model launches
stories.why_it_matters: Trump has signed an executive order requiring AI companies like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic to submit their new AI models for government pre-checking before public release. The idea is a compromise — tech giants get some regulatory certainty, while the MAGA base gets the optics of government oversight. Critics say it's not real regulation, just a tick-the-box exercise with no binding safety standards. For GOOG and MSFT, this adds a new bureaucratic step before launches but isn't the heavy-handed crackdown some feared.

stories.title: Microsoft builds its own AI models to cut reliance on OpenAI
stories.why_it_matters: Microsoft has unveiled a new family of its own AI models, developed in-house rather than licensed from OpenAI. The goal is to reduce how much Microsoft pays OpenAI for access to ChatGPT-style technology and to give developers cheaper options. This is a big strategic shift — Microsoft and OpenAI have been tight partners, but MSFT is clearly hedging its bets. In theory this is good for long-term MSFT margins, but the market sold the stock off last night — possibly spooked by what it signals about the OpenAI relationship.

stories.title: Is Google falling behind in AI? Commentary sharpens
stories.why_it_matters: Tech commentator M.G. Siegler has published a sharp critique arguing Google is now meaningfully behind OpenAI and Anthropic in the AI race. The core argument: the shift from AI features embedded in Google Search to standalone AI apps (like ChatGPT) is a structural challenge that Google is struggling to navigate, and missteps could be 'company-destroying.' This is the bear case for GOOG — not that AI is bad, but that Google might not win the AI era despite spending billions on it. Worth watching as a risk for your GOOG position.

stories.title: Google competing for $80 billion in investor money as big AI IPOs loom
stories.why_it_matters: Gizmodo reports that Google is suddenly competing for roughly $80 billion in investor funds that might otherwise flow into upcoming AI company IPOs (stock market listings). As OpenAI and Anthropic eye public listings, some investors who'd normally buy those IPOs may instead put money into Google as an AI proxy. This is actually a potential tailwind for GOOG — existing listed companies can attract capital when hot new listings aren't yet available.

sport.summary: NRL Round 14 kicks off tomorrow night. There's big coaching news at Manly, a Tigers star dropping a loyalty bombshell, and the AFL mid-season report cards are out. Warriors are on the bye this round.

stories.title: Kieran Foran appointed Manly Sea Eagles head coach
stories.why_it_matters: Former Manly and NRL veteran Kieran Foran has been handed the top job as Sea Eagles head coach. The news broke alongside a report that an Origin representative has signed with two clubs in one day — the player market is moving fast heading into the Origin period. Manly host the Rabbitohs tomorrow night at 4 Pines Park (7:50 PM) in what'll be Foran's first game in charge.

stories.title: 'I'll never be loyal to a club': Tigers star's shock warning, and why Benji is at the centre
stories.why_it_matters: A Wests Tigers star has publicly declared he'll never prioritise club loyalty over his own career — a direct shot that appears aimed at coach Benji Marshall and the club's management. The Tigers face Penrith Panthers on Sunday at CommBank Stadium. With this sort of instability in the camp, it's not great preparation heading into Round 14.

stories.title: NRL plots huge event to keep Jack Arrow from going to AFL
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL is reportedly planning a major promotional event around young star Jack Arrow to convince him to stick with rugby league rather than defect to the AFL. Arrow is seen as a generational talent and his potential crossover is a big deal for the code. The NRL clearly sees retaining him as worth a significant investment.

stories.title: AFL mid-season report cards: best players, biggest shocks
stories.why_it_matters: AFL.com.au has published mid-season report cards for every club, grading performance, identifying the best players and biggest surprises at the halfway point of the 2026 season. No article text was available, but if you follow the AFL this is worth a click for your club's verdict.
